newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks plunge on curbs, cash calls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks plunge on curbs, cash calls.

text.p: Malaysian blue-chip stocks bounced back on technical buying in the afternoon, but failed to recoup all the losses caused by brokerages making cash calls, new lending curbs and the overnight fall on Wall Street.

The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index plunged as much as 3.4 percent in the biggest intraday drop since March 21, 1994. It later recovered partially on selective blue-chip buying by British funds after 3.30 pm (0730 GMT).
Analysts said local funds also entered the market in the afternoon as blue chip buyers added to the rebound.
At the close, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks ended down 1.36 percent or 15.73 points at 1,136.78. The index had touched a low of 1,113.47.
"The selling was somewhat of an over-reaction. They were really bashed down," said Lynn Cheah Lee Ling, assistant manager of fund managers BHLB Asset Management in Kuala Lumpur.
Market volume surged to 459 million shares, valued at 2,763.48 million ringgit. Losers thumped gainers 555 to 130. Key banking, stockbrokerage and property issues were among the biggest losers.

Analysts said the factor that affected trading most was brokerages making cash calls on their customers -- asking them to top up their credit facilities -- after the nearly seven percent fall of the Composite Index this week.

Share prices have fallen throughout the week due to a plummeting market in New York and curbs by the Malaysian central bank, Bank Negara, on lending for property and stock purchases, the hottest sectors in the booming economy.
"The market is concerned about margin calls at the moment," said Soh Meng Hui, head of research at K.L. City Securities.
"There are some bad rumours of some stockbroking houses where punters have not been able to top up their margin calls, and have been forced to sell," he said.
New York's Dow Jones industrial average, always a major factor in Asian markets, set the bearish tone at the opening bell in Kuala Lumpur, after falling 39.66 points overnight.
Bank Negara's new guidelines, which took effect on April 1, limit financial institutions' lending to the property sector to no more than 20 percent of their total outstanding loans.

The central bank said it was maintaining a restriction on lending to finance purchases of stocks and mutual funds to 15 percent of an institution's portfolio and imposed new curbs on using shares as collateral to buy other shares.
In its annual report released last Friday, Bank Negara said it was concerned about speculative lending destabilising the banking system.
The banking system's exposure to the broad property sector stood at 29.1 percent of total loans at the end of February 1997. Lending to the sector expanded by 30.1 percent in 1996, the report said.
Lending by the banking system for purchases of shares increased 20.1 percent in 1996 to 26.1 billion, it said.
The market remained confused over how the measures would work despite a meeting on Thursday between Bank Negara and chief executives of banks to explain the lending curbs.
"A lot of next week's performance depends on what happens tonight (Friday) in the U.S., especially with non-farm payrolls and jobless data coming out," one dealer said.
"The long-term view for the Malaysian market is still positive, but in the short term we are negative," said Fiona Leong, head of research at J.M. Sassoon in Kuala Lumpur.
"My advice for next week would be to stay away from property stocks. They affect everything on the market from construction to plantations and banking stocks," said Cheah of BHLB.
